title: Lesson 7: Sustaining Momentum When Novelty Wears Off
description: Sustaining momentum when novelty wears off: the novelty effect and why the early spike is not the signal, how to tell real compounding momentum from a one-time spike, and the four-part cadence (resurface outcomes, remove friction, deepen with existing users, reward specific behavior) that keeps adoption alive after enthusiasm fades.

questions.question: Usage spikes during launch and falls sharply once the campaign ends. What does that indicate?
options: A novelty spike, because the usage depended on the event that started it
Compounding momentum, because usage was high at the very start of the quarter
A quality problem, because usage dropped after the launch
A licensing problem, because access was withdrawn too early
questions.explanation: Usage that collapses when the event stops was created by the event, while real momentum keeps running on its own returns.

questions.question: Which reading suggests momentum rather than a novelty spike?
options: High reach with high churn among people who tried it once
Steady reach with low churn and the same people returning
A sharp rise in sign-ups during the first week
A large number of one-time trials across many different departments
questions.explanation: Momentum shows up in depth and retention, the same people coming back, while a spike shows up in breadth and churn.

questions.question: Where is the cheapest next win when expanding adoption?
options: A large department that has shown no interest in the tool so far this year
A team made up of the most enthusiastic volunteers across the company
The existing users, through the next adjacent workflow
New hires who have never used the tool before
questions.explanation: Existing users already have access, the licensing, and the prompting skill, so the next adjacent workflow is a cheaper win than a cold audience.
